# Motivation

Let me share some Git workflow tips. Why do I need them? The fundamental reason
is that *development is faster than review*, and sometimes I don't like staying on
a single feature — I prefer working on several fronts concurrently. Maybe I get
bored easily, and I also believe: **a rough start is a good start**. So, absent any
special requirement, I like to *touch* every feature I plan to build. For developers
who face the same situation as I do, I want to share some hands-on experience with
Git workflows.

# Background

The worktree layout is:

- `main → smote → smotenc`, and now I want to create `smotenc-plus` based on `smotenc`.
- Another line: `main → smote → smoten`.

`smote` supports sample generation for continuous features, `smoten` supports
categorical features, and `smotenc` covers both.

`smotenc` is in fact under active development, but to demonstrate the workflow we
park the remaining work on `smotenc-plus`. The situation now: all the parts are
written, and only one *assembly* function — the synthetic-sample generator — is
missing. This time we need a function called `get_feature_wise_mode`. It is a helper
that takes the mode (most frequent value) of a categorical variable, and it lives on
the `smoten` branch, **not** on `smote`.

We also need a small change: following imblearn's logic, the old behavior on a tie
was to take a fixed, smallest feature — probably by the dictionary order of the
feature name. Now the `smotenc` implementation additionally needs to support
**random tie-breaking**, while keeping `smoten`'s "always take the smallest" logic
unchanged. This is easy: add a parameter with a default value, so that `smoten`'s
test code is untouched. As for *why* `smoten` and `smotenc` have this implementation
difference — I think it may be that the imblearn developers were a bit careless and
arbitrary. We won't worry about it for now; this post is only about demonstrating
the Git workflow.

Beyond the changes above, there is one major **structural** change:
`get_feature_wise_mode` originally lives on the `smoten` branch, but `smotenc` needs
it too. Both are child branches of `smote`, and their contents are invisible to each
other. But `smotenc` — and its own child branch — also need this
`get_feature_wise_mode`. So we want to **move it to the `smote` branch**, so that
every branch built on top of it — `smoten`, `smotenc`, and the grandchild branch
`smotenc-plus` — can all use it.

::: {.callout-important}
This point is important — remember it. It is the single biggest motivation for
writing this post.
:::

# Using worktree; the current branch situation

All branches are clean right now, with nothing uncommitted or unpushed, so we first
create the `smotenc-plus` worktree based on `smotenc`. worktree is a great practice:
it enables *truly parallel* development, which suits exactly this kind of
"several branches open and worked on in parallel" situation — far more convenient
than the stash-checkout-pop workflow.

```bash
git worktree add ../mlr3torchAUM-smotenc-plus -b smotenc-plus smotenc
```

This creates a sibling directory `mlr3torchAUM-smotenc-plus`; we enter that directory
to develop. Suppose we make a new commit on this branch. The commit history now looks
like:

```
f334ce7 (HEAD -> smotenc-plus, origin/smotenc-plus) delete the extra line
bcf7993 (origin/smotenc, smotenc) finish smotenc_distances
abe132c median_std function
b156163 complete split_features ant unit tests
52f31ac fix test
6b8d7d7 (origin/smote, smote) add knn_from_distance for both smoten and smotenc
7ae386b add guard for 0 query for knn_index and make_samples
```

The `smoten` branch (also present as a worktree in the sibling directory
`../mlr3torchAUM-smoten`):

```
204785b (HEAD -> smoten, origin/smoten) delete knn_index since it has been in smote
9e38281 doc
3f62365 misc
27ee6b5 complete SMOTEN class assembly
b71ca97 complete knn_from_distance
f05f087 complete sample_distances
9bd2845 finish feature_value_distances
8f3a03d finish make_samples_nominal
dce8494 complete feature wise mode function
6b8d7d7 (origin/smote, smote) add knn_from_distance for both smoten and smotenc
7ae386b add guard for 0 query for knn_index and make_samples
```

The structure is quite clear. Drawn as a diagram, it is:


# Change #2: rebase `smoten` + retire the function and tests

Switch to the `smoten` branch, and rebase onto `smote`:

```bash
git rebase smote
git log --oneline
```

```
ce57825 (HEAD -> smoten) delete knn_index since it has been in smote
5e77ec1 doc
5e607b8 misc
400b9f8 complete SMOTEN class assembly
0e23b0a complete knn_from_distance
989c42a complete sample_distances
b8adf61 finish feature_value_distances
33d0d5c finish make_samples_nominal
3462444 complete feature wise mode function
77fa4a7 (origin/smote, smote) add get_feature_wise_mode for both smoten and smotenc
6b8d7d7 add knn_from_distance for both smoten and smotenc
```

Before looking closely at this string of hashes, I noticed something odd in my
terminal:

```
~/code/r/mlr3torchAUM-smoten smoten ⇣⇡
```

See those up and down arrows? They mean the branch is simultaneously *behind* and
*ahead* of its remote! At this point I want to push, but it is rejected. What is
going on?

```
❯ git push
To github.com:mlr3-imbalanced/mlr3torchAUM.git
 ! [rejected]        smoten -> smoten (non-fast-forward)
error: failed to push some refs to 'github.com:mlr3-imbalanced/mlr3torchAUM.git'
hint: Updates were rejected because the tip of your current branch is behind
hint: its remote counterpart. If you want to integrate the remote changes,
hint: use 'git pull' before pushing again.
hint: See the 'Note about fast-forwards' in 'git push --help' for details.
```

Observing our commit hashes, we find:

**Before rebase + the remote state:**

```
204785b (HEAD -> smoten, origin/smoten) delete knn_index since it has been in smote
9e38281 doc
3f62365 misc
27ee6b5 complete SMOTEN class assembly
b71ca97 complete knn_from_distance
f05f087 complete sample_distances
9bd2845 finish feature_value_distances
8f3a03d finish make_samples_nominal
dce8494 complete feature wise mode function
6b8d7d7 add knn_from_distance for both smoten and smotenc
```

**After:**

```
ce57825 (HEAD -> smoten) delete knn_index since it has been in smote
5e77ec1 doc
5e607b8 misc
400b9f8 complete SMOTEN class assembly
0e23b0a complete knn_from_distance
989c42a complete sample_distances
b8adf61 finish feature_value_distances
33d0d5c finish make_samples_nominal
3462444 complete feature wise mode function
77fa4a7 (origin/smote, smote) add get_feature_wise_mode for both smoten and smotenc
6b8d7d7 add knn_from_distance for both smoten and smotenc
```

Every commit's hash *after* `complete feature wise mode function` has changed —
even though the commit messages and contents are exactly the same!

Drawn as a tree diagram:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  b6["6b8d7d7"]:::smote --> s77["77fa4a7 · get_feature_wise_mode<br/><b>smote</b>"]:::smote
  s77 --> ln1["3462444 · feature wise mode"]:::smoten
  ln1 --> lnd["⋯"]:::smoten
  lnd --> ln9["ce57825 · delete knn_index<br/><b>local smoten (HEAD)</b>"]:::smoten
  b6 --> on1["dce8494 · feature wise mode"]:::stale
  on1 --> ond["⋯"]:::stale
  ond --> on9["204785b · delete knn_index<br/><b>origin/smoten (old)</b>"]:::stale
  classDef smote fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#2563eb,color:#1e3a8a,stroke-width:2px
  classDef smoten fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#16a34a,color:#14532d,stroke-width:2px
  classDef stale fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#dc2626,color:#7f1d1d,stroke-width:2px,stroke-dasharray:5 3
```

From `6b8d7d7`, the remote forks off here; but locally we took one more step,
`77fa4a7`, which also shows that local and remote `smote` differ — and then it
forks off, having nothing to do with the remote anymore!

## Reading the reject message

**1. What does fast-forward mean?** The simplest, linear case: the remote's tip is
exactly an ancestor of the local tip — i.e. the most ordinary flow: you made some
commits locally and push them to the remote. Smooth. Everybody is happy.

**2. Should you `git pull`?** Never fall for the reject message's temptation! Let's
analyze what happens. Recall the tree diagram (the post-rebase divergence from the
previous section):

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  B["6b8d7d7<br/>(common ancestor B)"]:::smote
  B --> L["local smoten tip<br/>ce57825 (rebased, new)"]:::smoten
  B --> R["origin/smoten tip<br/>204785b (old)"]:::stale
  classDef smote fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#2563eb,color:#1e3a8a,stroke-width:2px
  classDef smoten fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#16a34a,color:#14532d,stroke-width:2px
  classDef stale fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#dc2626,color:#7f1d1d,stroke-width:2px,stroke-dasharray:5 3
```

`git pull` by default = `git fetch` + `git merge`: merge does **not** move, replace,
or stack any old commit; it only **adds one "two-parent" connecting node** that joins
the two lines — each grown independently from B — together at the top.

In fact, I never use merge; personally I only ever rebase. I want a linear commit
history.

That batch of work would then appear **twice** in the history (and, most likely,
conflict all the way through, because the same changes exist on both sides).
**Disaster!**

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  B["6b8d7d7 (B)"]:::smote
  B --> l1["77fa4a7 → 3462444 ⋯ ce57825<br/>local rebased (new hashes)"]:::smoten
  B --> r1["dce8494 ⋯ 204785b<br/>origin/smoten (old hashes)"]:::stale
  l1 --> M["MERGE commit<br/>(two parents · work appears twice)"]:::merge
  r1 --> M
  classDef smote fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#2563eb,color:#1e3a8a,stroke-width:2px
  classDef smoten fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#16a34a,color:#14532d,stroke-width:2px
  classDef stale fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#dc2626,color:#7f1d1d,stroke-width:2px,stroke-dasharray:5 3
  classDef merge fill:#fef9c3,stroke:#ca8a04,color:#713f12,stroke-width:3px
```

**3. `git push -f` — this is the correct posture.** It forcibly rewrites the remote
history to match the local one.

`-f` is short for `--force`. There is also `--force-with-lease`, which is safer and
suits the case where multiple people work on the current branch. I haven't run into
that case, so I won't go into it much — I'll cover it when I do. But
`--force-with-lease` also fits our situation, so the conclusion is: no matter what,
just mindlessly use `--force-with-lease`.

After the operation:

```
ce57825 (HEAD -> smoten, origin/smoten) delete knn_index since it has been in smote
5e77ec1 doc
5e607b8 misc
400b9f8 complete SMOTEN class assembly
0e23b0a complete knn_from_distance
989c42a complete sample_distances
b8adf61 finish feature_value_distances
33d0d5c finish make_samples_nominal
3462444 complete feature wise mode function
77fa4a7 (origin/smote, smote) add get_feature_wise_mode for both smoten and smotenc
```

Remote and local are forcibly aligned. We then safely retire this branch's
`get_feature_wise_mode` function; the tests still pass, because we have already
rebased onto the parent branch `smote`'s "all-in-one" `get_feature_wise_mode`.

Compared with the history before rebase:

```
abe132c median_std function
```

```{mermaid}

  b6["6b8d7d7"]:::smote --> s77["77fa4a7 · get_feature_wise_mode<br/><b>smote</b>"]:::smote
  s77 --> nnew["749d92f ⋯ f58926c<br/><b>local smotenc (rebased, new)</b>"]:::smotenc
```

# Change #4: `smotenc-plus` rebases `smotenc`

Now it's the grandchild branch `smotenc-plus`'s turn — it needs to rebase `smotenc`.
Its current commit history:

```
f334ce7 (HEAD -> smotenc-plus, origin/smotenc-plus) delete the extra line
bcf7993 finish smotenc_distances
abe132c median_std function
b156163 complete split_features ant unit tests
52f31ac fix test
6b8d7d7 add knn_from_distance for both smoten and smotenc
```

You may already have spotted the problem — the answer is that we should use
`rebase --onto`:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  S["S (6b8d7d7)"]:::smote --> X["X · get_feature_wise_mode (77fa4a7)<br/><b>smote</b>"]:::smote
  X --> ncnew["nc1' → nc2' → nc3' → nc4'<br/>749d92f ⋯ f58926c · <b>smotenc (new)</b>"]:::smotenc
  S --> onc["nc1 → nc2 → nc3 → nc4<br/>52f31ac ⋯ bcf7993 (old)"]:::stale
  onc --> p1["p1 · f334ce7 (delete the extra line)<br/><b>smotenc-plus</b>"]:::plus
  classDef smote fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#2563eb,color:#1e3a8a,stroke-width:2px
  classDef smotenc fill:#ffedd5,stroke:#ea580c,color:#7c2d12,stroke-width:2px
  classDef stale fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#dc2626,color:#7f1d1d,stroke-width:2px,stroke-dasharray:5 3
  classDef plus fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#4c1d95,stroke-width:2px
```

`--onto` lets you manually specify "from where to start replaying":

```bash
git rebase --onto smotenc  bcf7993  smotenc-plus
```

The full meaning of this command: we are currently working on `smotenc-plus`, and we
want to rebase onto `smotenc`'s latest tip; commit `bcf7993` and everything before it
on `smotenc-plus` — we don't care about those; we simply **replay the commits after
`bcf7993`** onto `smotenc`'s current latest tip.

What is `bcf7993`? It means: on the current `smotenc-plus`, `bcf7993` and the commits
before it are the ones we don't care about; we only look at what comes after it —
namely `f334ce7 delete the extra line` — which is the commit *unique* to
`smotenc-plus`.

This is the result we want: place `p1` on top of the new `smotenc`:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  S["S"]:::smote --> X["X (77fa4a7)<br/><b>smote</b>"]:::smote
  X --> ncnew["nc1' → nc2' → nc3' → nc4'<br/>f58926c · <b>smotenc (new)</b>"]:::smotenc
  ncnew --> p1new["p1' · f74ab50 (delete the extra line)<br/><b>smotenc-plus</b>"]:::plus
  classDef smote fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#2563eb,color:#1e3a8a,stroke-width:2px
  classDef smotenc fill:#ffedd5,stroke:#ea580c,color:#7c2d12,stroke-width:2px
  classDef plus fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#4c1d95,stroke-width:2px
```

Exactly the result we want.

## What modern Git does for us automatically

But let's actually try a direct rebase (without `--onto`):

```
~/code/r/mlr3torchAUM-smotenc-plus smotenc-plus
❯ git rebase smotenc
warning: skipped previously applied commit 52f31ac
warning: skipped previously applied commit b156163
warning: skipped previously applied commit abe132c
warning: skipped previously applied commit bcf7993
hint: use --reapply-cherry-picks to include skipped commits
hint: Disable this message with "git config set advice.skippedCherryPicks false"
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/smotenc-plus.
```

The result is fine — exactly what we want:

```
f74ab50 (HEAD -> smotenc-plus) delete the extra line
f58926c (origin/smotenc, smotenc) finish smotenc_distances
9777c08 median_std function
60aa283 complete split_features ant unit tests
749d92f fix test
77fa4a7 (origin/smote, smote) add get_feature_wise_mode for both smoten and smotenc
6b8d7d7 add knn_from_distance for both smoten and smotenc
```

What is going on? Those warning messages deserve attention. The skipped commits
correspond to the four commits before our commit:

```
bcf7993 finish smotenc_distances
abe132c median_std function
b156163 complete split_features ant unit tests
52f31ac fix test
```

They are the hashes committed by the parent branch `smotenc` *before* its rebase.
Once `smotenc` rebased onto `smote`, they became obsolete.

Modern Git has **automatic cherry-pick detection**: before replaying, it computes a
**patch-id** (a difference fingerprint) for each commit. It finds that the old commits
you are carrying:

```
bcf7993 finish smotenc_distances
abe132c median_std function
b156163 complete split_features ant unit tests
52f31ac fix test
```

have difference fingerprints **exactly identical** to those in the new `smotenc`:

```
f58926c (HEAD -> smotenc, origin/smotenc) finish smotenc_distances
9777c08 median_std function
60aa283 complete split_features ant unit tests
749d92f fix test
```

(even the commit messages are the same) → it judges "**these have already been
applied**" → **skips them automatically**, and replays only the genuinely new commit
that is truly unique to `smotenc-plus`:

```
f74ab50  delete the extra line
```

The source code for this is here:
<https://github.com/git/git/commit/767a4ca648f8791c1fb623bd9f79fd8d7f026499>

::: {.callout-warning}
So it is *conditional* — a smart Git feature. In general, **do not rely on it**;
mastering your Git history and using `--onto` for precise operations is the right
way.

And a final warning: do not fall for its temptation to use
`--reapply-cherry-picks` to include skipped commits — that replays the same content
again and creates a whole pile of conflicts!
:::

# Bonus: why does the same commit's hash change after a rebase?

In one sentence: **because its parent node changed. This is guaranteed.**

Some other things change too, such as the timestamp, the committer, and so on. A
commit's hash is derived by combining all of the above information.

By contrast, the **patch-id** mentioned earlier is computed *only* over the
difference in the committed file contents (`git diff`). That is why, earlier, when we
rebased the grandchild branch `smotenc-plus` onto `smotenc` *without* specifying
`--onto`, Git could recognize that these commits had already been applied and skip
them automatically.

# Summary

::: {.callout-tip}
- Don't use `git pull` / `git merge`; use `git rebase`.
- `git rebase` changes the commit history.
- You need to use `git push -f` and `git push --force-with-lease`.
- `git rebase --onto` solves the rebase problem for grandchild branches — and modern
  Git will, conditionally and intelligently, do this work for us.
:::
